# Evaluating and Red-Teaming AI-Assisted Systems {#sec-evaluating-agentic-architect}

::: {.epigraph}
> *"Measurements are key."*
>
> — H. James Harrington, *Business Process Improvement* (1991) [@Harrington1991BusinessProcess, p. 82]
:::

::: {.column-margin}
**Author's Note:** H. James Harrington, an author and quality engineer,
emphasized that systemic improvement requires well-defined measurement. In
AI-assisted hardware design, neither a good final design nor an efficient
search settles the question alone. The design shows what was achieved. The
complete workflow and its cost show whether AI improved how architects reached
it.
:::

::: {.callout-crux}
Does a complete AI-assisted workflow, including its technical system and human
decision work, improve architecture work over a credible alternative at
comparable total cost, and does that advantage survive deliberate challenge?
:::

An AI-assisted system can return an impressive candidate and still be
an engineering failure. The candidate may pass a fast simulator while failing
at a higher-fidelity tool stage. It may require more model calls, simulation
runs, formal checks, physical-design jobs, and expert repair than the
alternative it claims to improve. It may work only for one prompt, seed,
workload, or tool version. It may even alter a constraint or exploit a
checker instead of improving the design.

Evaluation must therefore distinguish four objects.

1. **Candidate design.** This is the proposed microarchitecture, RTL,
   configuration, script, mapping, or other design artifact. It is judged by
   function, constraints, architectural quality, implementation feasibility,
   and the work needed to integrate and maintain it.
2. **Method or component.** This is one learned or conventional method,
   retriever, predictor, generator, optimizer, wrapper, checker, or other named
   part. Its contribution requires a controlled replacement or an *ablation*,
   a test that removes or replaces that part while holding the surrounding
   system as fixed as the claim requires.
3. **Configured technical system.** This is the versioned combination of
   methods and components, represented design state, retrieval sources, routing
   rules, tool wrappers, automated checks, and stopping logic. It excludes
   human setup, intervention, review, repair, and decision work.
4. **Complete human-plus-technical workflow.** This combines the configured
   technical system with the architects, engineers, and reviewers who set up
   the task, intervene, interpret results, repair failures, approve changes,
   and decide when to stop.

A claim about one object does not automatically apply to another. A correct
candidate design does not prove that a method caused the result or that the
technical system is efficient. A reliable technical system does not prove that
the complete human-plus-technical workflow saves engineering time. A workflow
that helps on one study does not establish that its advantage survives a
different workload, design, tool, or implementation condition.

This chapter organizes evaluation around four connected questions.

1. **Architecture result.** Did the workflow produce a correct, feasible, and
   architecturally valuable design?
2. **Coordination, decision quality, and evidence use.** Did the workflow
   choose suitable methods and tools, maintain consistent state, interpret
   results correctly, and turn measurements into supported decisions?
3. **Total cost.** What did the work consume across models, data, tools,
   compute, licenses, elapsed time, failed attempts, and human effort?
4. **Reliability of the advantage.** Does any improvement persist across
   repeated runs and relevant changes in prompts, seeds, workloads, designs,
   tools, and operating conditions?

The two sets of four answer different parts of the same evaluation. The candidate
design is the primary object for the architecture-result question. A method or
component and the configured technical system are examined to explain
coordination, local resource use, and repeated behavior. The complete
human-plus-technical workflow is the matched object for total cost and the
reliability of an adoption advantage, while its candidate still carries the
architecture result. The evaluation must therefore name both the object being
compared and the difference it intends to measure. The effect of adopting a
complete workflow is not a component contribution, even when both analyses use
the same runs.

This chapter uses *red teaming* to mean deliberate tests that challenge the
requirements, measurements, tool path, component behavior, or stopping logic
that ordinary evaluation assumes will behave correctly. Those tests ask whether
the candidate or system can hide behavior, weaken its own checks, exploit
misleading feedback, spend without limit, resist interruption, or leave
corrupted state behind.

Verifying feedback inside one design study asks whether a particular
observation supports the next action. Complete-workflow evaluation asks a
broader question. Across tasks, runs, conditions, costs, people, and attacks,
does the assembled human-plus-technical workflow improve architecture work over
a credible alternative? This chapter focuses on that broader claim while
retaining feedback failures as one important source of error.

One successful run cannot settle these questions. A clean result may come from
a strong model, a conventional search method, a carefully engineered harness,
intensive human repair, or a benchmark that has become easy to exploit. A
failure may reveal a weak design, a poor method choice, a broken environment,
or an attack the system did not recognize. The evaluator must locate the
source rather than compressing everything into one score.

The output is a supported evaluation claim, not permission to tape out or
accept residual risk. The architecture-role discussion in
@sec-what-architect-owns explains who decides whether the design advances.

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}
After reading this chapter, you can:

- Distinguish the candidate design, method or component, configured technical
  system, and complete human-plus-technical workflow required for a fair
  comparison.
- Evaluate architecture results, coordination and decision quality, total
  cost, and the reliability of any measured advantage without collapsing them
  into one score.
- Compare an AI-assisted workflow with credible human-directed, conventional,
  retrieval-only, and model-based alternatives.
- Use repeated runs, varied conditions, budget curves, and component
  replacements to locate where an advantage holds, while keeping benchmarks
  current and comparable.
- Red-team an AI-assisted system for altered requirements, weakened
  checks, misleading feedback, hidden behavior, uncontrolled spending, and
  failed interruption or recovery, then state the supported scope and limits.
:::

## Defining the Evaluation Objects and Workflow Under Test

### Identifying the System Under Test

A benchmark score is never a property of a model alone. It belongs to the
whole system that received the task and produced the result. Retry logic,
retrieved material, prompts, and search policy are part of that system. Model
choice, tool access, feedback, and a human-supplied harness can materially
change the outcome [@WangEtAl2026ArchEval]. A comparison that names only the
model hides the engineering system under test.

The legal action space determines what the score means and what can go wrong.
Four common action spaces require different evidence.

- **RTL or intermediate-representation generation.** The system returns a new
  design artifact. Evaluation must cover function, blocking constraints,
  implementation feasibility, hidden behavior, structure, and the work needed
  to verify and change it.
- **Tool, script, or parameter tuning.** The system changes how an existing
  design is analyzed or implemented. Evaluation must preserve constraints,
  defaults, tool state, and stopping rules so that a cleaner report cannot come
  from silently changing the conditions.
- **Microarchitecture change.** The system changes queues, caches, arrays,
  interfaces, protocols, or another architectural mechanism. Evaluation must
  reach the affected workload, software, system boundary, implementation, and
  future integration consequences.
- **Test or constraint change.** The system changes a testbench, property,
  timing constraint, scoring script, or other part of the apparatus judging
  it. Any permitted change needs an evaluator-owned check that the system under
  test cannot modify.

A pass rate for generated RTL, a power, performance, and area (PPA) result from
parameter tuning, and a workload result from a microarchitecture change are not
interchangeable scores. They grant different powers and expose different
attack surfaces. Moving between action spaces creates a new evaluation
obligation, especially when the system can change the tests or constraints that
determine whether it passed.

The complete-workflow record should pin at least the elements in
@tbl-complete-system-identity.

| **Element** | **What the record must identify** | **Why it matters** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Evaluation object | Candidate design, method or component, configured technical system excluding human decision work, or complete human-plus-technical workflow | A result can be interpreted only at the level actually evaluated. |
| Learned components | Immutable model snapshot or endpoint identity where exposed, access date, mutable alias if used, inference settings, and any fine-tuning or adaptation | A changed model or setting creates a different system; an alias alone may not identify what ran. |
| Design information | Starting artifacts, retrieved sources with identities and versions, represented state, decision-relevant retrieval coverage, conflict handling, and update policy | Extra or fresher information can explain an apparent capability gain. |
| Methods and instructions | Generation, prediction, optimization, and composition rules; system and task instructions; prompt policy; retrieval and routing policy | The model may be one component in a stronger procedure, and changed instructions create a different configured system. |
| Legal action space | Which design, tool, script, parameter, test, and constraint changes are permitted | The allowed actions determine both the supported claim and the ways the system can alter its own evaluation. |
| Environment | Tool wrappers and schemas, executable tools, configurations, checkpoints, harness revision, runtime or container dependencies, and returned fields | The harness and runtime determine which actions are possible and which failures become visible. |
| Checks | Functional, architectural, physical, security, and acceptance checks | A result is only as strong as the checks it actually reached. |
| Human work | Setup, prompting, intervention, review, repair, and escalation roles | Hidden engineering effort can make an automated result look cheaper than it is. |
| Operating limits | Compute, tool, time, retry, and review budgets plus stopping rules | A system allowed more attempts or stronger tools is not a matched comparison. |

: **A complete-workflow identity extends beyond the model.** The record must
distinguish the evaluation object and make every material source of capability
and cost visible.
{#tbl-complete-system-identity tbl-colwidths="[18,42,40]"}

Use hashes or another immutable identity for prompts, retrieved snapshots,
starting artifacts, scripts, constraints, workloads, containers, and raw
records. Hosted model aliases and endpoints can change without changing their
names. When an immutable model snapshot is unavailable, record the access date
and state that exact model replay is unavailable.

Learned components, design information, and methods define where capability
may come from. The legal action space, environment, and checks define what the
configured technical system may change, which tools it can reach, and which
failures can become visible. Human work and operating limits then extend that
record to the complete workflow, exposing expert effort, compute, tool, retry,
elapsed-time, and review budgets that a model-only description would hide. This
identity makes versioned complete workflows comparable. It does not establish
that either workflow is better or isolate a component contribution.

The task and evaluation environment need a separate identity. At minimum, a
hardware result should name the design artifacts, workload and software path,
process design kit and cell library where relevant, constraints, tools and
versions, implementation stage, analysis corners, and acceptance rules.
Changing any of these may create a different result. A percentage measured on
an open 45\ nm library does not automatically transfer to a commercial node,
and a routed result is not a signoff result.

This separation between system identity and environment identity prevents two
common errors. The first is attributing the work of a carefully tuned harness
to its base model. The second is comparing two percentages that came from
different tasks, tool settings, or physical stages. Both can produce a
leaderboard, but neither establishes an architecture advantage.

### The Four-Part Evaluation Map

No single metric answers whether an AI-assisted system is good. The
useful question is which engineering decision a measurement can support and
what remains unknown. Four decision questions organize the measurements
without turning unlike quantities into one score
(@tbl-evaluation-metric-map).

| **Decision question** | **Measures to consider** | **What they reveal** | **What they cannot establish alone** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Is the architecture result supported? | Function and blocking constraints; performance, latency, and throughput; energy, power, and thermal behavior; area and product cost; security; implementation feasibility; maintainability; integration and verification burden; future change cost | What the candidate achieved, which requirements it met, and how deeply it was checked | Whether AI improved the work, whether the result repeats, or whether the organization should commit the design |
| Did the workflow make sound decisions? | Component-role selection; state consistency; tool and fidelity selection; interpretation accuracy; useful observations; supported decisions; false accepts and rejects; escalation, stopping, recovery, and human override | Whether the system coordinated its parts, interpreted tool results, and converted measurements into defensible architecture decisions | Whether the final design is good enough or whether the workflow is economical |
| What was the total cost? | Model calls and tokens; compiler builds; simulation, formal, synthesis, and physical-design runs; compute, memory, energy, and licenses; data and setup; failures and retries; elapsed time; human setup, diagnosis, review, and repair | Where resources were spent and whether a local speedup shifted cost or risk elsewhere | Whether the candidate is correct or which component caused a difference |
| Is the advantage reliable? | Repeated runs and uncertainty; calibration; worst cases and constraint violations; recovery; sensitivity to seeds, prompts, workloads, designs, tools, and operating conditions | How often an advantage repeats and the tested conditions in which it remains useful | Why the advantage holds or whether it transfers beyond the sampled tasks and conditions |

: **Metrics support different engineering decisions and should remain
separate.** Architecture results come first. Coordination, total cost, and
reliability explain how those results were reached and where an advantage
holds. Red-team tests cut across every row.
{#tbl-evaluation-metric-map tbl-colwidths="[20,36,22,22]"}

The rows are related but not interchangeable. A sound decision can still
produce a weak candidate when the search space is poor. A strong candidate can
hide an inefficient workflow. Low total cost cannot compensate for a result
that violates a blocking constraint. Red-team results do not form a fifth
score; they challenge the assumptions, interfaces, and checks behind all four
rows.

A practical evaluation uses the map in a fixed sequence. First, freeze the
architecture task, the system and alternative being compared, their legal
actions, budgets, and evaluator-owned checks. Second, run matched work while
retaining every attempt, failure, tool call, and human intervention. Third,
measure the architecture result, decision behavior, total resource use, and
reliability separately. Fourth, replace selected components and vary relevant
conditions to locate the source and limits of any advantage. Finally, attack
the assumptions and interfaces on which the result depends, then report the
claim as supported, unsupported, or unresolved. Later sections develop each
step; @sec-minimum-complete-workflow-protocol gathers them into a compact
protocol.

Naming a metric does not specify it. Every reported metric should identify the
event or outcome, experimental unit, target population and denominator,
evaluator-owned check and tool stage, budget or time window, aggregation and
failure policy, uncertainty, and treatment of censored runs. Architecture tasks
or decisions usually support generalization. Seeds, retries, candidates, tool
calls, and prompt samples are nested observations unless the claim and sampling
plan establish otherwise. More repeats inside ten tasks do not create more than
ten independent tasks.

The next sections define architecture result, decision behavior, and total
cost. Comparison design and component replacement provide the experiments
needed to estimate an advantage. Reliability then asks where that comparative
result repeats, while benchmark maintenance and red teaming challenge whether
it remains readable.

## Architecture Result

Architecture quality is not one scalar. A candidate must first satisfy the
functional requirements and every blocking constraint at the stated
evaluation stage. Among candidates that pass, the study can compare workload
performance, power, area, latency, cost, programmability, or other declared
objectives. If no candidate passes, the outcome is a failure at that stage, not
a low score to average away.

Select metrics from the intended decision rather than from a standard
checklist. Four groups are usually needed.

- **Correctness and blocking constraints** establish whether the candidate is
  eligible for comparison at all. They include functional checks, protocol and
  interface properties, timing and physical rules, security requirements, and
  any product constraint that cannot be traded away.
- **Architectural objectives** measure the quantities the decision is trying
  to improve, such as throughput, latency, energy, power, area, cost,
  programmability, or quality of service.
- **Implementation feasibility** records the deepest tool stage reached,
  analysis corners, congestion, timing, power delivery, thermal limits, and
  other evidence that the candidate can be realized. For a silicon-bound
  decision, it also covers manufacturability and yield assumptions,
  design-for-test and fault coverage, packaging, and the planned path through
  post-silicon bring-up.
- **Lifecycle burden** covers integration, verification, maintainability,
  traceability, and the work required to make likely future changes.

Verification coverage is part of the architecture result, but it is not a
correctness score. At the study level, map required behaviors and properties to
named checks, then report outcome category, applicable coverage, exclusions,
waivers, remaining holes, and any evaluator self-test used to show that the
apparatus detects plausible defects. @sec-feedback-verification-trust explains
what an individual simulation, formal, equivalence, or physical return can and
cannot establish. A high percentage cannot prove correctness, but a correctness
claim is not interpretable when the exercised behavior and untested
requirements are unknown. Keep this verification coverage separate from
benchmark coverage across the population of architecture tasks.

The outcome fields follow the problem rather than a universal metric list.
A processor or accelerator study may need workload coverage, throughput and
tail latency, compiler and runtime behavior, interface overhead, average and
peak power with a stated activity source, energy, area, floorplan and timing
results, thermal and power-delivery limits, reliability, security,
maintainability, integration status, verification burden, expected engineering
change order (ECO) work, and the deepest implementation stage reached. Omitting
a field does not make it irrelevant. It makes the corresponding claim
untested.

Multi-objective results should preserve the tradeoff rather than hide it in an
arbitrary weighted score. Report the feasible Pareto set or another explicit
tradeoff view, and identify dominated candidates [@Deb2001MultiObjective].
State how the final choice was made. If a reference Pareto front exists,
coverage and distance measures can show whether a search found one narrow
region or represented the broader tradeoff. If the reference is constructed
from the pooled candidates found by the evaluated systems, say so because the
measure is then relative to that pool, not absolute.

Maintainability and future change cost should remain inspectable rather than
being hidden inside a style score. Record whether the artifact is traceable to
the declared architecture, preserves understandable interfaces and module
boundaries, can enter the existing build and verification flow, and supports
the changes the product is likely to need. A change exercise can make the
burden concrete. Change a queue depth, interface field, timing target, or
security property, then record the design work, failed checks, verification
reruns, and affected modules needed to restore a supported result. A candidate
that wins PPA but turns every small ECO into broad manual repair is a weaker
architecture result, not merely a more expensive workflow.

Energy and power results need a measurement window, execution rate or work
completed, duty cycle, idle and leakage treatment, and the full boundary of
the claimed system. On-chip logic alone cannot support a subsystem-energy
claim that excludes the memory, interface, or regulator costs needed to
operate it.

Each reported quantity remains bound to its candidate, conditions, comparator,
uncertainty, check scope, and explicit nonclaims. A simulator result does not
become a silicon result because the workflow producing it was automated. A
trajectory that steadily reduces violations does not establish functional
correctness, physical feasibility, or a sound architectural mechanism.

For the Lighthouse target, the primary result is not a model or workflow score.
It is whether the checks support freezing an array and its interface under the
declared workload, software, memory, energy, and implementation conditions. A
local simulator result is one input to that decision. It does not settle the
implementation-facing result.

## Coordination, Decision Quality, and Evidence Use

An AI-assisted workflow does more than produce candidates. It selects which
component should act, what information that component should receive, which
tool and fidelity should be used next, how a result changes the represented
design state, and when the evidence is sufficient to stop or escalate. These
decisions can be wrong even when every individual model and tool works as
specified.

Evaluation should therefore reconstruct the sequence of architecture
decisions. For each consequential step, record the design question, the
available state, the action chosen, the expected observation, the result
returned, the interpretation applied, and the next decision. This is not a
request to save every internal token or private chain of thought. It is a
request to preserve the engineering information needed to understand why the
workflow changed the design or its conclusion.

Six failure classes deserve separate measurement.

1. **Role-selection failures** occur when the system uses generation where a
   lookup, predictor, optimizer, formal check, or human decision would have
   been more appropriate.
2. **State failures** occur when constraints, candidate identity, tool status,
   units, or prior results are dropped, duplicated, or carried to the wrong
   design.
3. **Information-use failures** occur when retrieval omits a
   decision-relevant source, uses the wrong version, hides conflicting sources,
   or returns material that does not support the downstream claim.
4. **Tool-selection failures** occur when the system uses an unsuitable tool
   or fidelity, repeats an uninformative run, or pays for a high-fidelity check
   before a cheaper test could reject the candidate.
5. **Interpretation failures** occur when the tool call completes but the
   workflow reads the result incorrectly, treats an inconclusive check as a
   pass, or attributes a change to the wrong mechanism.
6. **Control failures** occur when the system should stop, escalate, roll back,
   or request human review but instead continues or commits a bad state.

These distinctions prevent a common counting error. A completed tool call is
not necessarily a useful observation, and a useful observation is not
necessarily a supported decision. Report all three. Also report false accepts,
in which the workflow advances an invalid candidate, and false rejects, in
which it discards a candidate that an evaluator-owned check later shows was
viable. Parser failures, stale caches, incomplete logs, and corrupted state
belong in the same record because they affect the information available to the
workflow.

Tool-using behavior needs several rates rather than one autonomy score. Record
valid and authorized tool calls, useful observations per call and per unit
cost, first-attempt and retry success by failure class, repeated actions or
states, unsupported retries, stop-rule compliance, escalation accuracy on
evaluator-declared cases, intervention-free completion, human takeover, and
recovery of trusted state. A retry after a transient license failure is not
the same event as repeated repair of one conceptual mistake, so aggregate
retry counts remain secondary to their causes and outcomes.

Use declared opportunity sets for these rates. Measure stop-rule compliance
over runs that encounter a stopping condition, escalation accuracy over cases
with evaluator-defined escalation labels, intervention-free completion and
human takeover over assigned tasks eligible for the declared operating mode,
and recovery over failures for which the protocol requires restoration of
trusted state.

Retrieved information also needs positive quality measures. Record the identity
and version of each source, coverage of facts relevant to the decision,
unresolved conflicts, and whether the returned material actually supports the
claim that later steps make from it. An ablation can show that retrieval changed
an outcome, but it cannot establish that the information was current, complete,
or correctly used.

Decision quality should be compared against declared expected actions or
independent engineering review where such a reference can be established. For
ambiguous decisions, report reviewer agreement and the unresolved alternatives
instead of manufacturing one correct label. Calibration is also important. For
a predeclared binary outcome, such as whether a candidate passes one
evaluator-owned target check within a fixed evaluation horizon, a system that
assigns 80 percent confidence should see about 80 percent of held-out cases
reach that outcome under the tested conditions. Evaluate that relationship with a
calibration plot, a proper scoring rule, and a risk-coverage curve. A proper
scoring rule rewards useful probabilistic forecasts and penalizes confident
errors. A risk-coverage curve shows how the error rate changes as the system
handles more cases rather than abstaining or escalating. If the workflow does
not issue probabilities, evaluate when it abstains or escalates rather than
inventing a confidence measure.

Human support is part of the workflow, not an embarrassment to hide. Record
where people supplied missing context, corrected an interpretation, overrode a
decision, repaired an artifact, or stopped the run. Useful workflow metrics
include the fraction of decisions requiring support, time to a supported
decision, override rate, recovery rate, and the outcome after an override.
These measurements show whether AI reduced architectural work, moved it into
review and repair, or made expert intervention more effective.

## Total Cost

Four accounting rules organize this section. Count every attempt by tool type,
fidelity, outcome, and lineage, including failed and retried work. Preserve
human effort, model compute, tool use, licenses, energy, and elapsed time as a
resource vector instead of forcing them into one scalar. Separate one-time
setup and training from per-task cost, and separate active service demand from
queueing and schedule delay. Finally, compare total cost with a supported
architecture outcome or with the cost required to reach a predeclared outcome
threshold. A local speedup is not an efficiency result when it shifts cost or
risk into later checking and repair.

The cost classes in @tbl-total-system-cost extend beyond inference and EDA
calls. They include the work needed to prepare the task, make the environment
usable, inspect failures, verify outputs, recover from bad actions, and defend
the final recommendation. A local speedup can disappear when these costs move
downstream.

| **Cost class** | **Examples to record** |
| --- | --- |
| Human setup | Formulation, artifact preparation, environment integration, prompt and procedure development |
| Human operation | Supervision, intervention, failure triage, and manual design work |
| Human review and decision work | Independent checking, design review, documentation, approval preparation, and unresolved follow-up |
| Model and general compute | Model calls and tokens, inference time, accelerator time, training or adaptation, memory, storage, energy, and orchestration |
| Engineering tools | Compiler builds; invocations by tool type, fidelity, and final status; simulation runs and simulated cycles; formal, synthesis, physical-design, field-programmable gate array (FPGA) or emulation, and measurement resources; license checkout, wall time, and queue time |
| Data and samples | Workload traces, training or adaptation data, reference outputs, implementation samples, lab access, and silicon measurements where used |
| Verification and integration | Check development, proof and simulation work, debug, interface and software integration, regression, and evidence needed to close the result |
| Future change and ECO work | Expected design edits, affected modules and interfaces, verification reruns, implementation work, and specialist review for declared change scenarios |
| Failure and recovery | Invalid candidates, repeated runs, rollback, restored state, debugging, and rework |
| Schedule | Wall-clock time, time to a supported decision, critical-path delay, and variability in completion time |

: **Total cost includes the work before, during, and after the automated
search.** Report the categories separately unless a disclosed accounting rule
converts them to a common unit.
{#tbl-total-system-cost tbl-colwidths="[24,76]"}

Human work, machine resources, verification, future change, recovery, and
schedule remain separate accounting dimensions. A speedup in one can move cost
into another without lowering the total engineering burden.

Tool counts need fidelity, lineage, and cost composition. Report unique
configurations and seeds separately from invocation attempts. Give every
attempt an execution status, such as completed, crashed, timed out, canceled,
or license unavailable, and link every retry to the attempt that caused it.
Record the engineering result separately as passed, violated, infeasible, or
inconclusive. A formal timeout is not a falsification, and a place-and-route
crash is not evidence that the candidate is physically infeasible. Preserve
partial output, the allocated timeout, resources consumed, and failure
ownership. A timeout followed by a retry is two attempts, but it is not
automatically two independent configurations or two useful samples.

The operational execution and attempt record in
@sec-operational-attempt-record already captures identity, setup, status,
returns, cost, and lineage for every try. Comparative evaluation starts from
that record rather than defining another minimum schema. It adds the fields in
@tbl-attempt-cost-record so attempts can be assigned to comparison arms,
accounted for consistently, and interpreted without confusing an
infrastructure failure with an engineering result.

| **Evaluation field group** | **Fields added or made explicit for comparison** |
| --- | --- |
| Comparison placement | Comparison arm, paired task or block where used, candidate and attempt identifiers from the operational record, evaluator-owned stage and fidelity, and promotion or re-entry status |
| Engineering outcome | Passed, violated, infeasible, inconclusive, or not reached; properties or simulated cycles attempted, applicable coverage, reported waiver status, and deepest evidence stage |
| Censoring and disposition | Completed, crashed, timed out, canceled, or otherwise censored; censoring time and reason; partial output; and the declared rule for including the attempt in each analysis |
| Resources and cost | Model and tool calls; requested and consumed CPU core-hours, accelerator-hours, peak memory, storage and network use where material, measured energy, licensed feature identity and occupancy, whether allocated resources and licenses were released, queue and run time, retries, and recovery work |
| Recovery and state | State invalidated or restored, preserved descendants, and the attempt or checkpoint from which execution resumed |
| Human-work linkage | Active engineering minutes by role, independent review, intervention, adjudication, and passive waiting reported separately and linked to the affected attempt |

: **Evaluation extends the operational record rather than replacing it.** The
added fields separate comparison placement, engineering result,
censoring, total resource use, and linked human work for successful, failed,
retried, and censored attempts. A workflow therefore cannot erase cost or
difficulty by reporting only the candidates that finish.
{#tbl-attempt-cost-record tbl-colwidths="[22,78]"}

Candidate identity follows the declared design meaning, not the job identifier.
A meaning-changing repair or new design revision creates a new candidate with a
parent link to the design it revises. A retry or recovery that reruns the same
declared candidate and configuration after a timeout, license failure, or state
restoration keeps the candidate identity and creates a new attempt. When a
candidate re-enters a stage, its earlier stage membership and denominators do
not reset. The record retains the re-entry, attempt lineage, and any new parent
or child candidate identity.

The attempt record preserves every execution. A candidate funnel derives one
per-arm flow from those records by grouping attempts under unique candidate
identities. It does not create a second lineage or turn retries into new
candidates. The reusable schema in @tbl-candidate-funnel contains symbols, not
empirical results.

| **Funnel stage** | **Count and fractions to report per arm** | **Required denominators** | **Linked attrition and cost accounting** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Unique candidates proposed** | Count $U$; starting fraction $U/U$ | All unique candidate identities proposed or supplied to the arm | Proposal or acquisition cost, duplicate attempts, and candidates censored before eligibility review |
| **Low-fidelity eligibility** | Count $E$; $E/U$ | All unique candidates proposed | Eligibility-check identity and outcome, attrition reason, stage cost, retries, false accepts or rejects found later, and censoring |
| **Promoted or finalist** | Count $P$; $P/E$ and $P/U$ | Eligible candidates and all unique candidates proposed | Promotion rule, candidates not promoted by reason, selection cost, ties, retries, and censoring |
| **Higher-fidelity completion** | Count $H$; $H/P$ and $H/U$ | Promoted candidates and all unique candidates proposed | Completed check identity, noncompletion reason, stage cost, retries, timeouts, infrastructure failures, and censoring |
| **Blocking-check pass** | Count $B$; $B/H$ and $B/U$ | Higher-fidelity completions and all unique candidates proposed | Blocking-check identity, pass, violation, inconclusive or waiver status, false accepts or rejects found later, stage cost, retries, and censoring |
| **Final comparison and selection** | Counts $C$ compared and $S$ selected; $C/B$, $S/C$, and $S/U$ | Blocking-check passes, final comparison set, and all unique candidates proposed | Comparison and selection rule, dominated or unselected reason, final-stage cost, additional retries, censoring, and a declared no-selection outcome |

: **Candidate flow exposes where each comparison arm loses designs and spends
its budget.** Counts, fractions, denominators, reasons, retries, censoring, and
stage costs remain connected to the attempt lineage rather than being reported
only for finalists.
{#tbl-candidate-funnel tbl-colwidths="[18,23,24,35]"}

$U$ counts unique candidate identities, not tool invocations. $E$ records
those eligible after the declared cheap check,
and $P$ records those promoted. If a promoted candidate times out at the
higher-fidelity stage, it remains in the $P$ denominator and does not enter
$H$ unless a later linked retry completes. That successful retry still adds
only one completed candidate while every attempt and its cost remain in
@tbl-attempt-cost-record. $B$ records candidates that pass the blocking check,
and $C$ and $S$ record the final comparison set and selection. A run whose
observation window closes remains censored at its last reached stage. Reporting
these quantities for both arms reveals attrition and selection differences
that a finalist-only comparison would hide.

Shared human work needs its own work-episode identity. When one review,
meeting, or diagnosis covers several concurrent attempts, record the episode
once and link the affected attempts to it. Allocate that labor under a declared
rule or report it as shared work; do not charge the same minutes in full to
every attempt.

Aggregate study reports should retain the stage reached, check identity,
outcome category, cost, applicable coverage and waiver status, false accepts
and rejects found by evaluator-owned checks, and the number of candidates that
entered and left each stage. Keep analytical, simulation, formal, equivalence,
synthesis, physical-design, emulation, and hardware observations separate when
their costs and claim scopes differ. The tool-specific record behind those
fields follows the qualification rules in @sec-feedback-verification-trust.
One hundred model calls, one hundred cycle-level simulations, and one hundred
physical-design runs are not equivalent samples.

These quantities should not be collapsed carelessly. An hour of expert review,
an accelerator-hour, a license-hour, and a day of schedule delay are different
resources. Report the cost vector directly. A monetary total can be added when
labor rates, utilization assumptions, energy accounting, license accounting,
and treatment of shared infrastructure are disclosed. Every monetary summary
should also state its currency, valuation date or base year, and price source.
When currencies differ, state the exchange-rate source, date, and conversion
treatment. When those values are unavailable, report the resource vector rather
than inventing a precise total. The resource vector remains the primary record
even when a monetary summary is available.

Report intrinsic service demand separately from realized schedule. Service
demand includes active compute, memory, tool, and license occupancy. Realized
latency also includes queues, license denial, scheduler preemption, and
critical-path delay. State whether comparison arms ran concurrently, in
randomized time blocks, or under different infrastructure loads. Queueing is a
real operational cost, but it is also an apparatus condition that can make one
arm appear slower when the underlying service demand is unchanged. Do not sum
overlapping wall time, machine time, and license time as though they were one
resource.

Separate observed study cost, one-time integration and training cost, and
projected downstream product or lifecycle cost. Building a harness, integrating
a tool, preparing a prompt, calibrating a predictor, or training a model can
serve many later tasks, while each model call, simulator run, repair, and review
belongs to a particular task. Declare the expected usage horizon over which
setup and training are amortized and apply the same rule to both arms. If that
horizon is uncertain, report the comparison across several plausible task
counts. A standardized change exercise can measure maintenance work. An
unexecuted engineering change order remains a projection and should report its
estimation method and uncertainty rather than enter incurred cost as if it had
been observed.

Keep product outcome and workflow resource accounting in separate records.
Verification depth, integration status, maintainability, and expected ECO
burden can describe the quality and lifecycle consequences of a candidate.
Verification, integration, maintenance exercises, and ECO work can also consume
human, tool, license, compute, and schedule resources during the evaluated
workflow. The same activity may inform both views, but each consumed quantity
appears only once on a cost axis. Do not add a bundled verification or
integration charge when its underlying labor and tool use are already in the
resource vector, and do not add projected maintenance or ECO burden to observed
workflow cost for the same work. State whether each lifecycle quantity is an
observed outcome, an incurred resource, or a projection.

These records support two different efficiency claims. Complete workflow
efficiency relates a supported architecture outcome to the complete resource
budget, or reports the complete cost required to reach a predeclared supported
threshold. Sample efficiency is narrower. It measures supported architecture
improvement or decision resolution per evaluator-owned observation at a named
fidelity.
Analytical estimates, cycle-level and RTL or gate-level simulations, synthesis,
place-and-route, formal checks, FPGA or emulation runs, and hardware
measurements should be counted separately because they have different costs and
support different claims. A candidate, retry, or tool invocation is not
automatically an independent sample. Fewer tokens or tool calls establish only
a component saving unless architecture quality and complete workflow cost
remain comparable.

Hardware adds a steep evaluation cost [@Kahng2018Machine]. A model may spend
seconds proposing a tool-script change whose physical implementation takes
hours. More expensive reasoning can still be economical if it avoids enough
failed tool runs, but the trade must be measured rather than assumed. Report
quality as a function of total cost, identify non-dominated points on the
cost-quality frontier, and report the cost required to reach a predeclared
quality threshold. This preserves the useful lesson behind simulator-tax and
cost-quality plots without assuming that inference cost and tool cost always
form one universal curve.

The engineering comparison asks which complete workflow delivers the strongest
supported architecture result at each measured budget
(@fig-cost-quality-frontier). Each point represents a complete workflow, not a
model score. A point is dominated when another workflow reaches at least as
much supported design quality at lower total cost. The non-dominated frontier
preserves the choices that remain defensible. A predeclared quality threshold
then answers a different question, how much each workflow must spend before it
produces a candidate good enough for the architecture decision.

The vertical axis must represent one predeclared architecture outcome or an
explicit comparison rule for the declared objectives and constraints. It is
not permission to combine performance, power, area, correctness, and other
dimensions into an arbitrary hidden score.

```{python}
#| label: fig-cost-quality-frontier
#| fig-cap: |
#|   **A cost-quality frontier keeps one declared architecture outcome and one disclosed cost measure visible together.** The illustrative points assume a declared conversion into a synthetic cost index; measured studies should preserve the underlying resource vector. Filled points form the non-dominated frontier. Faded points cost more without producing a better supported result. The horizontal line marks a predeclared outcome threshold.
#| out-width: "82%"
#| fig-alt: "Illustrative scatter plot of total workflow cost against one normalized, predeclared architecture outcome. Four filled points form an increasing non-dominated frontier, three faded points are dominated, and a horizontal dashed line marks the predeclared outcome threshold."

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
from _python.plots import COLORS, apply_style

apply_style()

frontier_cost = np.array([1.0, 1.8, 3.0, 4.6])
frontier_quality = np.array([0.48, 0.67, 0.81, 0.89])
dominated_cost = np.array([2.4, 3.8, 5.2])
dominated_quality = np.array([0.56, 0.70, 0.83])
quality_threshold = 0.78

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.6, 3.1))
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.13, right=0.96, top=0.88, bottom=0.19)

ax.plot(
    frontier_cost,
    frontier_quality,
    color=COLORS["blue"],
    linewidth=1.8,
    zorder=2,
)
ax.scatter(
    frontier_cost,
    frontier_quality,
    color=COLORS["blue"],
    edgecolor="white",
    linewidth=0.8,
    s=42,
    label="Non-dominated workflows",
    zorder=3,
)
ax.scatter(
    dominated_cost,
    dominated_quality,
    color=COLORS["muted"],
    alpha=0.5,
    s=34,
    label="Dominated workflows",
    zorder=2,
)
ax.axhline(
    quality_threshold,
    color=COLORS["red"],
    linestyle="--",
    linewidth=1.2,
    label="Declared quality threshold",
)

ax.annotate(
    "lowest cost above threshold",
    xy=(3.0, 0.81),
    xytext=(3.35, 0.6),
    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color=COLORS["ink"], lw=0.8),
    fontsize=6,
    color=COLORS["ink"],
)

ax.set_title("Declared architecture outcome versus total workflow cost", fontsize=7.5, pad=10)
ax.set_xlabel("Disclosed illustrative cost index", fontsize=6.5)
ax.set_ylabel("Declared outcome (normalized)", fontsize=6.5)
ax.set_xlim(0.6, 5.6)
ax.set_ylim(0.4, 0.96)
ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=5.8, loc="lower right")
ax.tick_params(axis="both", labelsize=5.9, length=2.5, width=0.6, pad=2)
ax.grid(True, color=COLORS["grid"], linewidth=0.55, zorder=0)

for spine in ["top", "right"]:
    ax.spines[spine].set_visible(False)
ax.spines["left"].set_color(COLORS["ink"])
ax.spines["bottom"].set_color(COLORS["ink"])

plt.show()
```

The blue points improve supported quality as the disclosed cost index
increases, so none is strictly better on both axes. The gray points are
inferior to at least one blue point and should not anchor a claim of efficient
design. The dashed line changes the comparison from the best tradeoff to the
lowest cost that reaches an acceptable result. Real studies should plot
measured budgets and the predeclared architecture outcome, show uncertainty,
and preserve the underlying resource vector.

Here, a *program claim* is the cross-task claim that adopting the complete
workflow improves supported architecture outcomes, lowers total cost, or both
relative to the strongest practical alternative within the declared tasks,
conditions, budgets, and checks.

## Matching Complete Workflows

The program test in @sec-moonshot is stricter than “does an AI system produce
a valid design?” Full architectural success requires a supported design that
meets the fixed Lighthouse conditions. The effect of adopting the complete
AI-assisted workflow requires comparison with the strongest practical
conventional or human-directed workflow for the same question, declared
starting artifacts and source access, shared evaluation-tool access,
evaluator-owned acceptance checks, conditions, cost-accounting rule, budgets,
and stopping rules. The workflows may use different wrappers, internal checks,
procedures, or human work, but those differences remain part of the complete
workflow identity, effect, and cost. The workflow adds value only if it improves the
architecture result, lowers the total cost of reaching a result of comparable
quality, or both.

Useful comparison arms answer different questions. Random or enumerated search
tests whether guided search beats sampling. A strong conventional or
human-directed workflow tests whether AI assistance improves current practice.
A no-AI arm, retrieval-only assistance, foundation-model assistance, and the
fully configured workflow reveal how capability and cost change across
the system. No one baseline supports all of these claims.

Random search remains useful. It can expose a learned search that does no
better than sampling at the same budget. It is a diagnostic floor, not the
credible alternative an architecture team would otherwise use. Depending on
the task, that alternative may be direct enumeration, a deterministic
heuristic, a tuned optimizer, an existing EDA flow, or a human-directed study.
@sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization explains why the best
alternative follows from the represented problem rather than from a fixed
method hierarchy.

The two primary arms should obey the same comparison rules
(@tbl-matched-system-comparison).

| **Comparison element** | **Matching rule** |
| --- | --- |
| Evaluation object | Compare complete human-plus-technical workflows for the adoption estimate. Reserve method, component, or narrower AI contribution for a controlled replacement or ablation. |
| Architecture question | Ask both systems to resolve the same decision and preserve the same candidate and condition identities. |
| Starting information | Give both arms the same specifications, starting artifacts, workload information, prior results, and source access, except where access itself is the tested component. Record which sources each system actually consumes. |
| Development and tuning | Give both arms comparable opportunity, expertise, and budget for prompt, procedure, baseline, heuristic, parameter, and workflow tuning. Record inherited development effort and any remaining asymmetry. |
| Evaluation tools and checks | Give both arms access to the same evaluator-run tools and fidelity stages, and judge them with the same evaluator-owned acceptance checks and criteria. Treat workflow-internal tools and checks as system components, record their cost, and document any arm-specific access. |
| Budget | Use one cost-accounting window and compare at declared human, machine, tool, review, and elapsed-time budgets, preferably across several budget points rather than one arbitrary cutoff. |
| Human capability | Use practitioners with appropriate task knowledge in both arms and record their actions. Equal clock time does not make unequal expertise comparable. |
| Human-judged outcomes | Conceal arm identity and randomize review order where the artifact permits it. Record unavoidable cues, unblinded judgments, reviewer agreement, and adjudication. |
| Stopping rule | Apply the same success, failure, exhaustion, and timeout conditions. |
| Reporting | Publish the same architecture outcomes, failed runs, costs, and uncertainty for both arms. |

: **A matched comparison holds the architecture task and evidence standard
fixed.** Matching reduces alternative explanations and permits a qualified
estimate of complete-workflow differences under the declared assumptions.
{#tbl-matched-system-comparison tbl-colwidths="[22,78]"}

The workflows need not use identical internal methods, wrappers, checks, or
procedures because those differences are part of the workflow being evaluated.
They do need the same architecture question, evaluator-owned evidence standard,
declared resource window, and reporting rule. Matching reduces alternative
explanations without making unequal expertise or unreported access equivalent.
When wrappers, checks, procedures, or human work differ, the comparison does
not isolate a causal AI contribution.

A complete-workflow effect can be estimated when one declared
study feeds two complete human-plus-technical workflows and both arms report
results under the same evaluator-owned standard
(@fig-matched-complete-systems). The AI-assisted arm includes every learned
component, method, workflow tool, internal check, procedure, and human
intervention that contributes to the result. The alternative is the strongest
practical complete workflow the team would otherwise use, not a deliberately
weak baseline.

![**Matched complete workflows estimate the effect of adopting the whole
AI-assisted workflow.** The same architecture question and evaluator-owned
evidence standard feed an AI-assisted workflow and the strongest practical
alternative workflow. Each arm returns a supported architecture outcome or
declared failure, a resource-cost record, and results across repeated runs and
varied conditions, including failed runs. Task-paired differences support a
qualified complete-workflow effect conditional on the matching assumptions.
They do not isolate a component contribution.](images/F10-matched-complete-systems){#fig-matched-complete-systems
fig-alt="One declared architecture study feeds an AI-assisted complete
human-plus-technical workflow and the strongest practical complete workflow.
The comparison fixes the
architecture question, starting artifacts and source access, shared evaluation
tools, evaluator-owned acceptance checks, conditions, cost-accounting window,
budgets, stopping rules, and reporting requirements. Each workflow returns a
supported architecture outcome or declared failure, stated limits, a
resource-cost record, and results across repeated runs and varied conditions.
Failed runs remain part of those results. Task-paired differences estimate the
effect of adopting the whole AI-assisted workflow conditional on the
matching assumptions and tested envelope. They do not isolate a component or
AI contribution."
width="100%"}

The shared header fixes the comparison before the two arms diverge. Workflow
tools and internal checks may differ between the complete workflows being
compared, but the record exposes those differences. Each arm is a complete
human-plus-technical workflow rather than a model in isolation and can produce
either a supported outcome or a declared failure. Failed attempts remain in the
record. Qualified expertise, interventions, task assignment, and order are
recorded rather than assumed equivalent.

The comparison pairs the arms at the task level, then measures differences in
supported architecture outcome and total resources across repeated runs and
varied conditions. Those differences, their uncertainty, the matching
assumptions, and the tested envelope support a qualified estimate of the effect
of adopting the complete AI-assisted workflow. A mismatch between the
arms weakens that estimate. Isolating a method, component, or narrower AI
contribution requires the controlled replacements in the next section, and an
interaction that defeats isolation remains unresolved.

Before either arm runs, predeclare the primary architecture outcomes, required
task and condition coverage, acceptable total-cost envelope, minimum
worthwhile architecture improvement, and noninferiority margin for a
cost-reduction claim, meaning the largest acceptable loss in architecture
quality when the cost falls. Also state how many paired tasks and repeats are needed
to distinguish those margins with useful precision. Without these rules, a
study can call an imperceptible gain successful after seeing it or accept a
cheaper result whose architecture quality has materially fallen.

The task population and sampling rule also belong in the predeclared study
plan.
Name the class of architecture decisions the program claim covers, then state
how tasks, workloads, implementation conditions, and repeats are sampled from
it. Adaptive prompt development, method tuning, and search may use a
development set. The primary program comparison should use held-out tasks and
conditions that did not guide those choices, followed by evaluator-owned
confirmation of any selected architecture result.

Exploratory configuration development and confirmatory evaluation must remain
separate [@NosekEtAl2018Preregistration]. Record how many prompts, models,
routing policies, metrics, task variants, and analysis choices were tried before
the final comparison. Name the primary outcome and analysis before opening the
holdout. If adaptive search across configurations or outcomes could explain the
reported advantage, use a fresh confirmation set rather than treating the
selected result as confirmatory [@DworkEtAl2015ReusableHoldout]. Apply the same
development opportunity and accounting rule to the strongest practical
alternative. A mature baseline may carry inherited tuning, but the study must
record that advantage rather than tune only the AI-assisted arm and call the
result matched.

When people direct either arm, assign tasks with a declared balancing or
randomization rule and record who worked on which task. If the same person
uses both systems, rotate the order and account for knowledge carried from the
first arm into the second. If different people are used, match relevant
experience and report the remaining difference. These controls do not make
expertise identical. They make the human comparison interpretable. Give both
arms a declared familiarization period and a stable operating procedure.
Separate familiarization from measured task time. When the first arm reveals
design information that would advantage the second, use fresh tasks, a
declared washout, or an analysis that treats the carryover explicitly.

For human-judged outcomes such as maintainability or explanation quality, hide
arm labels and randomize review order where feasible. Some artifacts reveal
their origin through style or structure. Record those cues, any unblinded
judgment, reviewer agreement, and the adjudication procedure rather than
claiming blinding that the evaluator could not maintain.

Every assigned run remains in the result. An incomplete design, timeout, tool
failure, or exhausted budget receives its declared result status and cost rather
than disappearing because it produced no final score. Results restricted to
successful runs can be reported as a secondary view, but they cannot replace
the all-assigned comparison on which the program claim depends.

A timeout is a failure when the outcome is success within a fixed budget. It is
right-censored when the outcome is time to a supported result, meaning the
completion time is known only to exceed the timeout. The analysis should not
discard either case or assign a fabricated completion time.

A single equal-budget comparison can still conceal the important result. One
system may find a better design only by spending much more, while another may
reach an adequate design quickly. Budget sweeps reveal the cost-quality
relationship. For each arm, report the best supported architecture outcome
reached as human effort, model compute, tool use, and elapsed time increase.
Points dominated on both outcome and cost need no further defense.
Report both quality at comparable total cost and the total cost required to
reach a predeclared quality threshold. Either view alone can favor one part of
the relationship.

“Comparable total cost” needs a declared accounting rule. One option is a
resource envelope that limits human effort, model compute, tool use, review,
and elapsed time separately, then compares systems by outcome and resource
dominance. Another is a disclosed conversion to a common unit using stated
labor, compute, license, and schedule assumptions together with the currency,
valuation date or base year, price source, and exchange treatment established
earlier. Without one of these rules, two resource vectors cannot be called
equal merely because each was summarized as “cost.”

The architecture-result and total-cost definitions established earlier now
apply identically to both arms. A cheap invalid design is not a cost win, and a
good design does not by itself show that AI improved the work. The next step is
to estimate the complete-workflow effect and then locate which methods or
components it depends on.

## Complete-Workflow Effects and Component Contributions

The matched strongest-practical comparison estimates the effect of adopting the
AI-assisted workflow as a whole. It does not show which method or
component produced the difference. Controlled replacements and ablations
address that second question by removing or replacing one material part while
keeping the surrounding technical system, human procedure, task, checks,
budgets, and reporting fixed as far as the claim requires. Each replacement
supports only a dependency or contribution claim under that comparison
(@tbl-system-ablations).

| **Component under test** | **Useful comparison** | **Claim the comparison can support** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Complete AI-assisted workflow | Compare with the strongest practical alternative workflow under the same task, evidence standard, and total-cost accounting | The effect of adopting the whole workflow on result quality or cost, not an isolated AI contribution |
| Foundation model | Replace it with retrieval-only assistance, a smaller model, or another declared model while preserving the surrounding workflow | Whether the measured result depends on that model capability and its cost |
| Generation | Replace generated candidates with the same-size human, rule-based, or existing candidate set | Whether generation changed candidate quality or diversity at the declared cost |
| Prediction | Remove the learned screen or replace it with a conventional proxy and send a matched sample to the higher-fidelity check | Whether prediction saved evaluation work without discarding decisive candidates |
| Optimization | Replace the search policy with the strongest practical conventional method at matched budgets | Whether the optimizer improved the cost-quality relationship |
| Retrieved design information | Remove, freeze, or substitute the retrieval source while preserving the remaining system; check source versions, decision-relevant coverage, conflicts, and local claim support | Whether retrieved material changed results and which source dependencies remain |
| Routing and role selection | Replace adaptive routing with a fixed sequence or evaluator-declared component choice | Whether dynamic method and tool selection improved decisions or merely added complexity |
| Tool feedback | Restrict or delay selected feedback fields while keeping tool stages fixed | Which returned information enables correction and which merely adds cost |
| Automated checking | Replace one checker with an independently developed check where feasible | Whether the conclusion depends on one checker or one shared assumption |
| Human intervention | Compare declared intervention policies and record every intervention | How much human work is necessary for the measured result |

: **Ablations locate dependencies inside the complete workflow.** They do not
turn an interacting workflow into independent additive contributions.
{#tbl-system-ablations tbl-colwidths="[20,45,35]"}

The complete-workflow comparison estimates the effect of adopting the whole
workflow. Controlled replacements then test whether that result depends on a
particular foundation model; generation, prediction, or optimization method;
information source; routing policy; feedback channel; automated check; or
human-intervention policy. Equalize tool budgets when the question concerns
method quality. Allow budgets to differ, but count them, when the question
concerns complete-workflow efficiency. Each claim remains limited to the
component or complete workflow that the comparison actually changed.

One-at-a-time replacement is not a guarantee of causal isolation. Components
interact. A predictor may help only with one optimizer, and a model may appear
strong only because a human repairs its tool calls. A practical evaluation
starts with the components most likely to explain the measured advantage,
tests selected interactions when conclusions change, and reports the
dependencies it cannot separate. If interaction with wrappers, checks,
procedures, or human work prevents isolation, the component or AI contribution
remains unresolved. Contributions are not additive. The gain from replacing
several interacting parts cannot be reconstructed by summing one-at-a-time
differences.

## Reliability Across Conditions

A single stochastic run is an anecdote, not a measurement
[@HendersonEtAl2018DeepRL]. Repeated runs estimate reliability under the same
task. Varied conditions test whether the result survives the changes that
matter to an architecture decision. Both are necessary.

Reliability is broader than average success. Report worst cases, blocking
constraint violations, recovery after failure, time and human support required
to recover, and the fraction of decisions that experts override. Test whether
reported confidence is calibrated to eventual results. A workflow that is
correct 90 percent of the time but is most confident on its failures presents
a different engineering risk from one with the same pass rate and useful
uncertainty estimates.

The earlier decision-quality test covers confidence in workflow outcomes.
Numerical architecture estimates need a different calibration record. Report
interval coverage, interval sharpness, and errors near the decision boundary,
each tied to a tool stage, time horizon, and condition distribution.
Calibration on one workload, node, design family, or toolchain does not imply
calibration after that condition changes.

### Separating System Variation From Apparatus Variation

Pair the arms on tasks, controlled tool factors, and declared starting
conditions. Treat model or search seeds as repeats under one fixed configured
system. A changed prompt is usually a changed system configuration. Prompt
samples are exchangeable repeats only when a predeclared prompt-sampling policy
is itself part of the system under test. None of these is an independent
architecture task. Report successes, failures, constraint violations,
recoveries, median,
interquartile range, and per-task results. Means and standard
deviations can hide hardware studies whose outcomes are bimodal, with one
group of runs failing implementation and another finding a strong design.

The evaluation apparatus can vary too. Placement seeds and tool settings can
change a physical-design fit [@Altera2026QuartusFitter], while logically neutral
build or environment changes can perturb measured performance
[@Mytkowicz2009WrongData]. Identical reruns test whether a nominally fixed setup
is repeatable. Separate sensitivity studies deliberately vary one of these
factors. Do not subtract environment variance from model variance as if they
were automatically independent. Predeclare whether the comparison estimates an
average over the declared apparatus factors, a result at one fixed setup, or a
worst case.
Estimate that quantity and its interval with a design that can separate the
factors where possible. If the system difference cannot be distinguished from
the apparatus-induced difference at the required practical margin, the result
remains unresolved.

`pass@k` can describe whether at least one of $k$ exchangeable generated
candidates produces a binary pass. Report it with the estimator and sampling
convention used
[@Chen2021Codex]. In hardware it also needs a time or tool budget, since one
success among many expensive failures may be unusable. Deployment reliability
asks a different question, how often an ordinary run succeeds, not whether at
least one of many attempts eventually worked. Neither score says anything
about physical validity beyond the check used to define “pass.”

Statistical analysis should match the data and the claim. Paired comparisons
are useful when both systems run on the same tasks and conditions, but the
corresponding nonparametric tests still rely on paired observations and
independent task units [@Demsar2006StatisticalComparisons]. Bootstrap intervals
can summarize skewed statistics, but additional resamples do not repair a small
or unrepresentative task set.^[Bootstrap
resampling repeatedly draws observed experimental units with replacement to
estimate variation in a statistic. Paired observations require paired
resampling. Time-dependent observations require block resampling that preserves
local dependence [@Kunsch1989BlockBootstrap].] Report the realized sample size,
failures, effect sizes, intervals, and the analysis choice rather than treating
one test as mandatory.

A study that claims performance across a sampled task population should treat
architecture tasks as the primary generalization units, pair systems within
task and condition, and treat repeated runs as nested observations rather than
extra tasks [@AgarwalEtAl2021StatisticalPrecipice]. A fixed finite suite or
convenience sample supports only the population it actually represents. Report
per-task effects and the across-task effect when the sampled task population
justifies it,
uncertainty, failures, and practical decision margins.
Analyze seeds, retries, and conditions according to their nested relationship
without treating them as independent tasks. Keep exploratory configuration
selection separate from held-out confirmation, and declare how multiple
outcomes or subgroup comparisons affect the decision rule.

### Varying Architecture-Relevant Conditions

A scaling study must name the architecture difficulty axis. Useful axes include
the legal design-space size, the number and coupling of constraints, tool-flow
depth, feedback cost, and cross-layer span. Report supported outcomes, failures,
human intervention, reliability, and total resource cost against that axis.
Model size and task count may be experimental settings, but neither establishes
that the architecture problem became harder.

The varied conditions from @sec-loop-patterns-across-stack become an
evaluation matrix rather than background description
(@tbl-lighthouse-evaluation-matrix).

| **Condition varied** | **What remains fixed** | **Failure the variation can expose** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Workload and input distribution | Architecture question, candidate identities, and required functions | A gain limited to the synthetic or easiest workload |
| Compiler, runtime, and mapping | Hardware candidates and system constraints | A hardware result that depends on one software path |
| Interface and traffic assumptions | Functional contract and candidate set | A local gain erased by communication or synchronization cost |
| Memory and energy model | Workload and mapping identities | A candidate selected through an incomplete subsystem model |
| Implementation stage and corner | RTL intent and acceptance properties | A simulated gain that disappears in synthesis, routing, power, or signoff analysis |
| Tool version and configuration | Task and declared design space | A conclusion tied to one tool behavior or hidden default |
| Prompt, model, or routing configuration | Task, legal actions, tools, and acceptance checks | An apparent architecture advantage that depends on one phrasing or component choice |
| Source and represented-state freshness | Task, legal actions, evaluator-owned checks, and current project artifacts | A decision based on stale specifications, constraints, tool guidance, or project state |

: **Architecture-relevant variation tests where an advantage holds.** Each
material change either receives a test or remains an explicit untested
boundary.
{#tbl-lighthouse-evaluation-matrix tbl-colwidths="[25,36,39]"}

The fixed conditions isolate the failure attributable to each declared
variation. A result that disappears under one row narrows the tested envelope.
It does not explain every other condition or transfer to an untested one.

One task cannot support a program-wide claim. A useful suite spans distinct
architecture decisions, workloads, designs, result costs, representations,
tool stages, and failure consequences. Report the envelope in which the
advantage repeats, the conditions where it disappears, the worst observed
case, and the cases not tested. Also report whether failures were detected
before an invalid candidate advanced and whether the workflow recovered
without expert repair. That is empirical generalization. Similar-looking
artifacts are not enough.

Four levels of claims should remain distinct. Repeated runs measure stochastic
behavior on the same task. Here, *robustness* means stability under declared,
meaning-preserving changes that should not alter the correct architecture
result. Input-preserving apparatus or representation perturbations test that
robustness around the configured system; a changed prompt,
representation semantics, or tool policy may instead define a different
system. Held-out tasks support generalization within a declared design
population only when their sampling or selection represents that population
and they remained outside system and evaluator selection. A convenience
holdout is merely unseen. A new design family, toolchain, process node,
organization, or decision class is a transfer claim and needs a new target
evaluation. Performance and calibration must be re-estimated at each level.
Cross these conditions selectively, such as workload with compiler or design
with physical corner, when their interaction is part of the architecture risk.

## Benchmark Health and Comparable Results

Benchmarks make comparisons repeatable, but they do not remove the need for
architecture judgment. Their job in this chapter is to instantiate the metric
map for a declared task, action space, and evidence depth. SPEC CPU, PARSEC, and
MLPerf became useful because they defined workloads, rules, and reporting
conventions that made results more comparable [@PARSEC;
@SPEC2017CPU; @MattsonEtAl2020MLPerf]. An AI-assisted architecture benchmark must define both
the design problem and the system allowed to work on it. Its score remains one
instrument inside the complete-workflow evaluation.

Existing hardware-generation suites illuminate parts of the problem.
VerilogEval evaluates whether a model can generate functionally correct
Verilog from a specification [@VerilogEval;
@PinckneyEtAl2024RevisitingVerilogEval]. RTLLM broadens the designs and reports
syntax, functional, and post-synthesis quality-of-result measures [@RTLLM].
ArchEval evaluates architecture challenges across several simulators and
harness-support settings while recording system trajectories
[@WangEtAl2026ArchEval]. ChiPBench evaluates chip-placement methods through a
common physical-design flow [@WangEtAl2025ChiPBench]. Two recent preprints
connect more of that path. HSCO-Bench exercises hardware-software co-design
through FPGA-deployed SoC prototypes [@TsaiEtAl2026HSCOBench]. CLOSER-Bench
couples front-end and back-end closure tasks and records simulator, synthesis,
static timing, and place-and-route invocations together with final quality,
progress over budget, tool cost, and cross-stage recovery
[@ZhouEtAl2026CLOSERBench]. These are useful building blocks, but each remains
limited to its declared tasks, platforms, tools, and checks. None alone
establishes that a complete AI-assisted workflow improves an architecture
program over its credible alternative.

### Pinning the Task, Action Space, and Fidelity

A benchmark release should identify the following elements without redefining
the action spaces established earlier.

- the architecture question, artifacts, workloads, software path, legal action
  space, and permitted design or evaluation changes;
- the process design kit, libraries, macros, floorplan, utilization, activity
  source, constraints, scripts, defaults, tools, versions, hosts, threads,
  seeds, modes, and analysis corners where relevant;
- the functional, implementation, security, and acceptance checks, plus the
  information visible to the system and the feedback returned after each
  action;
- human intervention rules, budgets, stopping rules, failure treatment; and
- the scoring, aggregation, refresh, and retirement conventions.

Evaluator-owned requirements, rejection checks, and scoring rules should be
immutable to the system under test. When modification of a constraint,
testbench, or tool script is itself part of the task, an independent
evaluator-owned check must determine whether the change remains legal.

Task selection determines what the benchmark can represent. Remove exact and
near-duplicate tasks across development and evaluation splits, preserve
distinct design families rather than many variants of one easy block, and
state the architecture population the suite is intended to sample. Keep
hidden tests and evaluator-owned holdouts for properties that should not be
optimized directly, but document their categories and failure rules well
enough that the task remains an engineering problem rather than a guessing
game.

Benchmark validity is an inference from tasks to a claim, not a property of the
score alone. Three questions make that inference concrete. Do evaluator-owned
checks measure success on the declared task? Does the score capture the claimed
architecture capability rather than syntax repair, harness familiarity, or
checker exploitation? Do the task distribution, artifacts, feedback, budgets,
and human interactions resemble the design programs to which the result is
applied? A claim-to-task map should connect each program claim to sampled
decisions, failure consequences, and evidence stages. Gaps in that map become
limits on the claim rather than hidden assumptions.

The deepest completed evaluation stage bounds the claim. Report the stage,
check identity, outcome category, cost, coverage and waiver status, and
candidate flow, then apply the check-specific scope from
@sec-feedback-verification-trust. Passing an earlier stage supports only the
claims that stage can test.

This hierarchy also shapes cost. It is often wasteful to send malformed RTL
directly into a long physical flow. A benchmark may use cheap checks before
expensive ones, but it must report which candidates reached each stage and
must not score a cheap proxy as though it were the stronger check. State
checkpoints can reduce repeated setup cost, provided both arms receive
equivalent access and the restored tool state is part of the system record.
Cached results must be keyed by the complete environment manifest, not only
the RTL hash, because a changed constraint, library, floorplan, activity file,
or tool version creates a different evaluation.

The evaluator also needs tests for its own apparatus. Seed benchmark releases
with known-good and known-bad designs, differential-test important checkers,
and inspect disagreements among simulators, formal tools, synthesis, and
physical-design stages. A checker bug or simulator exploit can make an invalid
